title: Assess the quality of avocados for export

lessons.title: The avocado export industry, its terms and requirements
lessons.html:
Background and structure

South African avocados are grown mainly in Limpopo (around Tzaneen and Levubu), Mpumalanga (around Nelspruit, Hazyview and White River) and KwaZulu-Natal, with newer plantings in the Western Cape. A large share of the crop is exported, historically mostly to Europe and the UK, with growing interest in other markets. The industry body is the South African Avocado Growers' Association (SAAGA), which falls under the subtropical fruit umbrella organisation Subtrop together with mango and litchi growers.

The main export cultivars are Hass and other dark-skinned types, and green-skins such as Fuerte, Pinkerton, Ryan and Edranol. The chain runs from growers through packhouses, cold stores, exporters and shipping lines to ripening centres and retailers overseas. Many avocados are ripened by the importer before sale.

Terminology

  • Dry matter (DM) / moisture content: the main maturity index for avocados. Dry matter rises as oil content increases; fruit picked below the minimum will not ripen with good flavour.
  • Count: number of fruit per carton, related to fruit mass.
  • Green-skin and black-skin (Hass type) cultivars, which have different colour expectations.
  • Lenticel damage: dark spots on the skin from handling or wet fruit.
  • Cold damage / chilling injury: skin browning or pitting from too-low temperatures.
  • Anthracnose and stem-end rot: fungal decays that develop during ripening.
  • Vascular browning and grey pulp: internal disorders.

Legislative and logistical requirements

Avocados for export are regulated under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990, which sets maturity, class, packing and marking requirements. PPECB inspects under that Act and oversees the cold chain under the PPECB Act 9 of 1983. Importing countries may impose phytosanitary requirements and registration of orchards and packhouses. Retailers usually require GLOBALG.A.P. certification and residue compliance.

Logistically, avocados travel mainly by sea in reefer containers. Exporters must schedule harvests so fruit is mature, avoid harvesting wet fruit, cool promptly, pack to count and get the consignment to port within the planned window.

lessons.title: Sampling and judging external and internal quality
lessons.html:
Drawing a representative sample

  • Use the sample size in the export standards for the number of cartons offered.
  • Draw cartons at random across pallets and positions in the stack.
  • Check that the declared cultivar, count and class on the carton match the contents.
  • Record pallet and carton identification so results can be traced to PUC and packhouse.

External quality

For each fruit, check:

  • Mass and count within the declared range, and uniformity in the carton.
  • Shape: typical of the cultivar; misshapen or necked fruit is limited by class.
  • Skin blemishes: wind scarring, sunburn, hail marks, thrips damage, and healed marks. Class tolerances limit total blemished area.
  • Lenticel damage and bruising from rough handling.
  • Pests: scale, mealybug and any signs of fruit fly or other quarantine pests.
  • Stem: cleanly cut to the specified length; pulled stems leave open wounds that invite stem-end rot.
  • Skin colour: green-skins should be green and firm; Hass at export is usually still green, not already turning black.

Internal quality

  • Dry matter is determined by taking flesh samples, weighing them, drying them and weighing again. The result is compared with the minimum for the cultivar.
  • Firmness: export fruit should be hard and unripe.
  • Internal disorders: cut fruit and look for vascular browning, grey pulp, pulp spot and early decay.
  • Ripening test: some programmes ripen a sample to check for anthracnose, stem-end rot and disorders that only show when soft.

Avocados ripen after harvest and their internal problems often appear only at the importer's ripening room. Careful assessment, including ripened samples where required, helps catch a problem before the whole consignment fails overseas.

lessons.title: Cold chain protocols and the consignment outcome
lessons.html:
Monitoring the cold chain

Avocados are climacteric and very sensitive to temperature. Too warm, and they ripen and soften on the ship. Too cold, and they show chilling injury such as skin browning and grey pulp. Exporters therefore follow temperature regimes worked out by industry research for each cultivar and stage of the season, sometimes with stepped temperatures during the voyage. Controlled atmosphere containers are often used to slow ripening further.

Points to monitor:

  • Time from harvest to cooling: fruit should not stand in the sun or wait long before cooling.
  • Pulp temperature with a calibrated probe before loading.
  • Container set points and CA settings against the shipping instruction.
  • Data logger placement in the container.
  • Container pre-cooling, cleanliness and seal condition.
  • Ethylene: keep avocados away from ripe fruit and ethylene sources before shipping.

Determining the outcome

  1. Check that dry matter meets the minimum for the cultivar. Immature fruit fails regardless of appearance.
  2. Calculate external defect percentages and compare with class tolerances.
  3. Assess internal disorders and decay against tolerances.
  4. Confirm packing, marking and registration codes are correct.
  5. Decide pass, downgrade where allowed, or reject, and record the reasons.

A typical rejection scenario: a block of Fuerte is picked early to catch prices, but dry matter is below the minimum. Even if the fruit looks perfect, it fails and cannot be exported until it matures. Another: fruit picked wet after rain shows lenticel damage above tolerance and is downgraded.

Report findings clearly and factually so the packhouse can correct the cause, such as harvesting practices, handling or grading.

Key points

  • SAAGA, under Subtrop, represents avocado growers.
  • Dry matter is the key maturity measure for export avocados.
  • Pulled stems, wet harvesting and rough handling cause rot and lenticel damage.
  • Avocados suffer both from warmth (ripening) and from chilling injury.
  • Immature fruit fails inspection no matter how good it looks.
